name: Topilutamide (Fluridil)

lead: Topilutamide (fluridil) is a scalp-applied antiandrogen sold as Eucapil in the Czech Republic and Slovakia for pattern hair loss in men and women. People interested in topical alternatives to oral DHT blockers discuss it.

It blocks the androgen receptor in the scalp, so follicles are less affected by DHT and thin more slowly. It is reported to break down quickly in human serum. Published data consists of small older studies and lab work; no large randomized trials were found.

paras: It is used as a 2% lotion applied to the scalp, regularly over months. Users often pair it with other hair-loss measures.
Safety data are limited. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA for hair loss.

angle.text: Topilutamide blocks androgen receptors at the scalp, so follicles shrink less under DHT and thinning slows. Users interested in topical options instead of oral DHT blockers discuss it. It is sold in two European countries, and published trial data is small.

lead: Topilutamide, also called fluridil (code BP-766), is a topical nonsteroidal antiandrogen applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss in men and women. The idea is to block androgen receptors in the scalp itself so that follicles are less affected by DHT, helping hair stay thicker without changing hormone levels elsewhere in the body. It is marketed as a 2% product, Eucapil, by Interpharma Praha.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes it as approved for cosmetic use in Europe and sold only in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with no FDA or EMA approval for androgenetic alopecia.[1] Its design is that it is hydrophobic, applies locally and breaks down in blood serum, which is the basis for claims of low systemic exposure.[1][3]

A 2002 study in Dermatologic Surgery reported that in 43 men with androgenetic alopecia, 2% fluridil raised the anagen (growth-phase) percentage of hairs from 76% to 85% at three months and 87% at nine months versus no change on placebo.[3] On T Nation, hair-loss threads list fluridil as an alternative to finasteride and RU58841, with posters noting limited information and a poor cost-to-benefit ratio.[4][5]

paras: Topilutamide is used on the scalp for androgenetic alopecia [1]. Wikipedia notes that finasteride and minoxidil are the only drugs approved for the condition in major jurisdictions, and that topilutamide lacks FDA and EMA approval for it [1].

It is an androgen receptor antagonist of the perfluoroacylamido-arylpropanamide class, structurally related to flutamide and bicalutamide [1]. Wikipedia reports that it has higher receptor affinity than bicalutamide and hydroxyflutamide and suppressed androgen receptor by about 96% in prostate cancer cells at 10 micromolar, but notes that these findings need validation. It degrades in human serum with a half-life of about 6 hours, and breakdown products were undetectable in human serum in studies, which is the basis for claims of low systemic exposure [1].

A 2002 report in Dermatologic Surgery described a first clinical experience. Twenty men wore occlusive forearm patches for 21 days with 2, 4 and 6% fluridil and vehicle controls; fluridil showed no sensitization or irritation potential. In 43 men with Norwood II-Va androgenetic alopecia, 2% fluridil was tested in a double-blind placebo-controlled study: average anagen percentage was unchanged in placebo subjects but rose from 76% to 85% in fluridil subjects at three months and to 87% at nine months, and former placebo subjects rose from 76% to 85% after six months of fluridil. Sexual function, libido, blood counts and blood chemistry stayed normal.[3]

Wikipedia also mentions a 9-month open study in women and a further clinical study in men, both described as showing benefit and safety, without quantitative detail.[1] Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, reports the women's study as 11 women with Ludwig I-II alopecia showing an increase in hair diameter; this has not been checked against the primary paper.[2] The studies are small and from the early 2000s; larger randomized trials were not found.
Topilutamide was developed in the late 1990s by Biophysica, Inc., according to Grokipedia, introduced for medical use in 2003, and its patent expired in 2020.[1][2]

A 2007 T Nation hair-treatment thread names fluridil (Eucapil) as something the poster had learned little about and understood to have a longer-acting effect, while a 2009 thread about finasteride and testosterone lists fluridil and RU alongside other options whose cost-to-benefit ratio the poster rates poorly.[4][5] These are personal views, and neither thread reports trial data.

lore.intro: Fluridil is mentioned in T Nation hair-loss threads as a lesser-known alternative to finasteride and RU58841.[4][5]

claims.claim: Topical fluridil can replace systemic DHT blockers.
Fluridil is too costly or little-known to be worth the effort.

timeline.event: First clinical experience with topical fluridil published in Dermatologic Surgery.[3]
